title: Using Tanner Spectral Reduction to Improve Multi-Layer Optical Lattice Routing for Hypergraph-Product and Bivariate Bicycle qLDPC Codes
abstract: We characterize the Tanner graph spectrum of hypergraph-product (HGP) / lifted-product (LP) codes and bivariate-bicycle (BB) codes, informing qubit routing for three-dimensional reconfigurable qubit architectures. Syndrome-extraction routing depth on HGP/LP Tanner graphs reduces to a single SVD on the base parity-check matrix, using a spectral ratio $β_\text{HGP} = (1 + β_\text{base})/2$ where $β_\text{base} = σ_2(H)/σ_1(H)$ for the base parity-check matrix, and a diameter identity $D_T = 2 D_\text{base}$ where $D_\text{base}$ is the base Tanner graph diameter. Fourier spectral reduction reveals that the BB Tanner graph spectrum equals the union, over the $l \times m$ grid of characters of $\mathbb{Z}_l \times \mathbb{Z}_m$, of the singular values of a single $2 \times 2$ symbol matrix built from the two defining polynomials. This reduces spectral analysis from an $O((lm)^3)$ diagonalization of the $4lm$-node Tanner graph to $lm$ independent $2 \times 2$ SVDs. These results compose into a multi-layer three-dimensional AOL routing protocol with one-time setup cost $T_\text{Valiant} = O(\log N)$ atom rearrangements amortizable over a memory experiment of $R$ rounds. For a Tanner graph chromatic index $χ'$ and $L_\text{layers}$ stacked AOL planes, the per-syndrome-cycle depth is $\lceil χ'/L_\text{layers} \rceil$ AOL pattern activations with no atom motion, an $8\times$ step-count reduction at $L_\text{layers} \geq χ' = 8$. Contingent on multi-layer AOL hardware, this yields an estimated $\sim50-300\times$ per-cycle wall-clock advantage over a single-layer AOD baseline (degrading to $\sim5-100\times$ under AOD-crosstalk overhead), reducing to equality in the single-layer limit. This paper therefore presents a route toward practical routing improvement for future quantum hardware incorporating multi-layer reconfigurable qubit architectures.
summary: This paper develops a novel multi-layer routing protocol for qLDPC codes designed for future optical quantum hardware. It uses advanced spectral graph theory to simplify the analysis of complex Tanner graphs associated with HGP and BB codes. The resulting architecture promises substantial improvements in per-cycle operation speed compared to existing single-layer methods.
main_problem: The primary goal is to improve qubit routing efficiency for quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) codes by analyzing their underlying Tanner graph structure.
main_result: The authors propose a multi-layer optical lattice routing protocol that achieves significant per-cycle wall-clock speedups ($\sim 50-300	imes$) compared to single-layer methods, contingent on advanced hardware.
method: The work employs spectral analysis (SVD and Fourier transforms) to characterize the Tanner graph spectrum of HGP and BB codes, leading to simplified routing depth calculations for a multi-layer architecture.
model_or_system: The model involves three-dimensional reconfigurable qubit architectures utilizing optical lattices (AOL/AOD) to implement qLDPC codes like Hypergraph-Product (HGP) and Bivariate Bicycle (BB).
key_observables: Spectral ratio ($ eta$), Tanner graph diameter ($D_T$), chromatic index ($\chi'$), and per-cycle syndrome extraction depth.
important_parameters: Number of layers ($L_{	ext{layers}}$), base matrix singular values ($\sigma_k$), and the setup cost $T_{Valiant} = O(\log N)$.
main_assumptions: The results are contingent on the availability of multi-layer AOL hardware, and some theoretical bounds rely on unverified hypotheses (H1–H3).
figures_summary: Not specified in detail; notes reference spectral visualizations for HGP codes showing eigenvalue matching.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first characterizing the spectra of HGP/LP and BB codes using advanced spectral techniques, deriving simplified formulas for routing depth bounds. It then constructs a multi-layer 3D AOL routing protocol based on these findings, culminating in performance estimates compared to single-layer baselines.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the physical implementation challenges of large-scale quantum computation by providing theoretical speedups and architectural blueprints for qubit connectivity.
